ch1.testimonial: I am writing to tell you how strongly I feel about SignWriting and how much it can benefit Deaf people. I was born Deaf to a Deaf family and I am a native American Sign Language (ASL) user. I have been working with SignWriting since 1982. I was the first Deaf person to write articles in ASL, in SignWriting, for the SignWriter Newspaper. Later, Valerie Sutton and I established the Deaf Action Committee for SignWriting (the DAC) in 1988. I think it is very important to spread the word about SignWriting. ASL is a language in its own right, yet until the development of SignWriting, it was a language without a written form. When I found out about SignWriting I was thrilled to think that at last we would have a way to write our language. Deaf Americans are one of the very few linguistic minorities that are unable to get books teaching English in their native language. I feel that we can use SignWriting in order to learn English. Deaf people will benefit greatly from books explaining English grammar and idioms in written ASL. We can also use it to write down and preserve our stories, poetry and plays. As you know, there are many Deaf playwrights and poets, and up until now, they have not had a way to write the ASL in their literature. No matter what the project, SignWriting encourages us to read and write and I feel that is important. All of us hope that you will enjoy learning SignWriting. Your interest and support is a great help to our Deaf community.

ch12.shoulderLineIntro: Everything in this chapter is built on the shoulder line — a horizontal bar across the shoulders. From it the body lifts, moves, tilts, bends and twists. Click any symbol below to see it in every direction.
ch12.shouldersIntro: The shoulders hold a position — one or both raised or lowered — or move up and down on the Wall Plane, or forward and back on the Floor Plane.
ch12.torsoIntro: The whole upper body stretches up or sinks down, curves and bends to the side, twists left or right, or tilts from the ribcage.
ch12.tiltsSubhead: Rocking Motion from the Hip Joint
ch12.tiltsIntro: The upper body tilts or rocks back and forth. The neck and torso do not bend — they stay straight, moving as a unit from the hip joints.

ch11.rimBack: Rim of the Back of the Head
ch11.rimTop: Rim of the Top of the Head
ch11.rimSide: Rim of the Side of the Head
ch11.headIntro: The Head is written as a circle, read from different viewpoints — front, back, side or top — shown by small marks on the rim: a nose triangle for a side view, a bar or diamond for a top view, a double arc for the back.
ch11.contactIntro: A Contact Center star marks the spot where contact is made. It sits in the middle of any viewpoint.
ch11.rimIntro: The Rim marks a place on the edge of the head. Each rim symbol rotates to eight positions around the circle, naming a spot on the face, the back, the top or the side of the head. Click a symbol to see every position.
ch11.relatingIntro: A rim symbol written beside a sign means the hand is relating to that part of the head.
ch11.movementIntro: Click a movement symbol to see it rotated into every direction. Extra arrowheads on the symbol show the movement repeating or going back and forth.
ch11.headDirectionIntro: The entire head travels in the direction of the arrows. The nose remains straight and the neck does not bend.
ch11.faceDirectionIntro: The nose moves in the direction of the arrows. The neck bends and stretches as the nose moves.
ch11.faceLinesIntro: This is not movement — it is a stable position. The horizontal bar is the shoulders; the stem marks the direction the nose and face point, relating to the shoulders. One symbol writes the nose pointing up or down; the other adds a head tilt. Click to see every position.

punctuation.term: QUESTIONING PAUSE BEFORE END OF PHRASE
punctuation.english: similar to a Question Mark in English
punctuation.detail: When a sentence or phrase ends in a question, there is a slight pause at the end. The semi-colon symbol is used to write that pause at the end, but it must be combined with signs that write the grammatically necessary Facial Expressions and Head Movements that occur in sign languages when asking questions, including Head Forward and Eyebrows Up or Down.

punctuation.english: similar to a Colon in English
punctuation.detail: This is used in the middle of a sentence, marking a new phrase that lists items 1, 2, 3 and so on.
Marks a second thought inside a sentence, starting with the curved-up symbol and ending in the curved-down parentheses.

ch14.dyn1: SignWriting, like other writing systems, has punctuation. A dark line at the end of a SignWriting sentence is the equivalent to a period in English. It marks the end of the sentence or phrase. Two lines represent a pause, or comma.
ch14.dyn2: SignWriting can add more feeling to sentences by adding Dynamics Symbols to the Punctuation.
ch14.dyn3: The Fast Symbol represents a sentence executed quickly, with speed. This is similar to an Exclamation Point in English.
ch14.dyn4: Slow, Smooth, Tense and Relaxed Dynamic Symbols can also be placed near Punctuation Symbols to give the feeling of slow, smooth, tense or relaxed sentences.
ch14.readingIntro: Punctuation in context, written in vertical SignWriting columns. The Period and Pause lines close each thought; the annotations mark the Facial Expressions, Head Movements and Dynamics that carry the meaning.

ch10.intro: Facial expressions are written inside the Facial Circle. Each feature — the forehead, eyebrows, eyes, eyegaze, ears, cheeks, nose, breathing, mouth, tongue, teeth and chin — has its own group of symbols placed where it sits on the face.
ch10.neutralText: The empty circle is the face seen straight on. Every expression is built by adding symbols to it.
ch10.convention: Right and left, both at once. Paired features — eyebrows, eyes, ears, cheeks — are written for both sides, the right side alone, or the left side alone (right and left are the signer’s own). Directional features — eyegaze, tongue, chin — are rotated to point where they go. Click any symbol below to see its variants.
ch10.sideHint: Both at once, the right side alone, or the left side alone.

intros.eyebrows: Eyebrows are written above the eyes. The straight eyebrows lift up, rest neutral, or pull down; the dreamy eyebrows curve.
intros.eyegaze: Eyegaze shows where the eyes look. Wall-plane gaze moves up and down the front wall; floor-plane gaze moves forward and back.
intros.chin: The jaw moves on two planes: wall-plane chin movement points up and down, floor-plane chin movement points forward and back.

ch13.caption: Dynamics symbols mark the speed, timing and quality of movement, handshapes, faces and whole phrases.
categories: Movement Dynamics are small symbols placed near movement arrows. They indicate movement that is fast, slow, smooth, tense, relaxed, simultaneous, alternating, and uneven-alternating.
Handshape Dynamics mark classifiers. They mark a hand that is held in one place for a long time.
Facial Dynamics show tense or relaxed facial muscles. The Tense Symbol is used for lips that press together, for raised cheeks, and for squeezed eyes.
Punctuation Dynamics show the speed, timing and quality of entire phrases and sentences.
Unit Dynamics marks the influence of one symbol on a whole group of signs. The Unit-Connecting Line is used to show one facial expression influencing several signs.

movement.title: Simultaneous Line
movement.body: Both hands move at the same time.

movement.title: Alternating Lines
movement.body: The right hand moves in one direction, while the left moves simultaneously in the opposite direction.

movement.title: Un-Even Alternating — One Moves While The Other One Is Still
movement.body: The right hand moves while the left remains still. Then the left moves while the right remains still.

ch13.cl1: Classifiers are written with the handshape, plus a Classifier Marker. The Classifier Marker is a Tension Symbol. It is placed under the handshape.
ch13.cl2: In this sentence, Goldilocks sees a bowl of porridge. The bowl is established in space by a feeling of tension, a little like the feeling of placing something on a table. It anchors the visual picture of a bowl in space. The Tension Symbol marks that feeling. It is always placed under the handshapes.
ch13.cl3: Once the classifier is established, one hand continues to mark the classifier, held in the same position, while the other hand does other signs. The Tension Symbol remains under the hand that marks the classifier.
ch13.cl4: Goldilocks is discussing the porridge. She is saying that she sees the bowl, and then eats the porridge from it. But the porridge is too hot!!
ch13.facialHeading: Facial Dynamics Related To Handshape Dynamics
ch13.fac1: Facial expressions are essential to writing Sign Language stories and literature. They mark grammar and emphasis. The Tense Lips symbol shows the dynamics of the lips tensing as the hand is established in space by a classifier. Tension on the lips and near the hands are oftentimes written together.
ch13.fac2: Below: The Classifier for "bed" in American Sign Language is written with a Tension Symbol under the handshape to mark the classifier. At the same time, the lips also tense, giving the feeling of "anchoring the classifier" in space.
bedPlacements: This bed is placed to the left side. It is established in the left space, to the left of the facial expression. The lips tense as the classifier is placed in space.
This bed is placed in the center. It is established in the center space, directly under the facial expression. The lips tense as the classifier is placed in space.
This bed is placed to the right side. It is established in the right space, to the right of the facial expression. The lips tense as the classifier is placed in space.

ch13.u1: Influence is written with a Unit-Connecting Line.
ch13.u2: The Unit-Connecting Line is useful for Sign Language researchers. It is used to show the influence of one facial expression on a group of signs.
ch13.u3: When one symbol influences a group of symbols or signs, the symbol that is influencing the group is written first. Then a line is written, like a bracket, connecting the symbol with the group it influences.
ch13.u4: When SignWriting is written vertically, the Unit-Connecting Line is written to the side of the vertical column, as shown here. The Unit Line is grey or lighter than the signs.
ch13.u5: In Spain, the Unit-Connecting Line is used for horizontal SignWriting literature. When writing horizontally, the Unit-Connecting Line is written under or over the writing.
ch13.u6: In Sutton DanceWriting, the Unit-Connecting Line is used often to show the influence of one movement symbol on a group of other symbols. In SignWriting, it is rarely used for everyday use.
